catalog_quote: With the exception of the monosyllabic particles, that are either enclitic or proclitic, each word in Coos has its stress accent, designated by the acute mark (') or by the rising tone rendered here by ^. The former accent is not inseparably associated with any particular syllable of a word. It may, especially in cases of polysyllabic stems, be shifted freely from one syllable to another, although it is very possible that this apparent shifting of accent may be largely due to the rapidity with which the words in question were pronounced by the natives. The circumflex accent appears mostly on the last syllable, and may best be compared with the intonation given to the word so in the English interrogative sentence Is that so ? audit.reasoning: Quote check: verbatim at Frachtenberg 1922 sec. 5 p.309 in both copies we hold (scanned and PDF text layer, PDF p.23). Deciding source is the language's only reference grammar, and both StressTyp2 (LEX, same page) and WALS cite nothing else for stress, so the record is correctly sourced and the lexical/no-rule reading follows the text (no placement rule; one accent-type minimal pair). It is not 'well-sourced' in the strong sense because the statement is a 1914 impressionistic note that itself hedges ('apparent shifting.. may be largely due to rapidity'), and a later dedicated phonemic study (Pierce 1971, Linguistics 9(75):31-42) exists unread; that article is the one item that could refine the classification (e.g. to phonemic-lexical vs. non-contrastive/right-edge).
